sec.title: Background
sec.p: Glioblastoma is an aggressive brain cancer with a 5-year survival rate of 5–10%. Current therapeutic options are limited, due in part to drug exclusion by the blood–brain barrier, restricting access of targeted drugs to the tumor. The receptor for the type 1 insulin-like growth factor (IGF-1R) was identified as a therapeutic target in glioblastoma. We previously reported that the intracerebral growth of glioma cells with reduced IGF-1R levels was inhibited. The objectives of this study were to evaluate the sensitivity of glioma cells to a novel IGF-axis inhibitor, the IGF-Trap, and optimize its delivery to the brain.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We tested the effect of the IGF-Trap on the growth of the human glioma stem cells MES-1123 and U87 MG cells, and of murine GL261 cells in vivo, using subcutaneous and orthotopic implantation.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: We show that the growth of glioma cells implanted subcutaneously or orthotopically in the brain was inhibited by systemic and direct intracerebral administration of IGF-Trap, respectively, resulting in increased survival. To increase the efficiency of systemic delivery to the brain, we encapsulated the IGF-Trap in trimethyl chitosan (TRIOZAN™) nanoparticles prior to intravenous injection. We found that nanoparticle encapsulation increased the uptake and retention of the IGF-Trap in the brain and resulted in an improved therapeutic effect against intra-cerebrally growing tumors.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Our results identify the IGF-Trap as a potent inhibitor of intracerebral glioma growth and show that encapsulation in nanoparticles can improve delivery of biologics such as the IGF-Trap to the brain, thereby enhancing the therapeutic response.
Keywords: drug delivery, glioblastoma, IGF-Trap, nanoparticles, targeted therapy

boxed-text.p: The clinical management of glioma has been hampered by limited access of targeted biologics to the tumor site, due to exclusion by the blood–brain barrier (BBB). Effective treatment of glioma, therefore, faces the double challenge of identifying drugs that target specific drivers of glioma growth in vivo and successfully delivering those inhibitors to the tumor site to curtail its growth. In the present study, we aimed to address both of these challenges. Our results identify blockade of the IGF-axis as an effective therapeutic strategy to inhibit intracerebral glioma growth. They also show that encapsulation of this biologic in TRIOZAN, a trimethyl chitosan-based nanoparticle, increased the efficiency of its systemic delivery to the brain and enhanced its therapeutic effect in an orthotopic murine glioma model. These results have translational implications for the treatment of glioma but may also be more broadly relevant for the management of other brain tumors, including brain metastases from other primary malignancies.

body.p: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most prevalent primary brain tumor in adults. Glioblastoma occurs at higher rates in persons older than 55 years of age and the 5-year survival rate for GBM patients is a dismal 5–10%.1 Morphological and molecular characterization of GBM identify this malignancy as poorly differentiated and highly heterogeneous with 3 major subtypes the proneural, classical, and mesenchymal subtypes each enriched for specific somatic alterations.2 Altered oncogenic pathways include copy number alterations in the tyrosine kinase receptors signaling pathways, epigenetic changes in retinoblastoma (Rb) gene expression and genetic mutation as well as copy number alterations in p53.3 Tyrosine kinase receptors such as the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR), and type 1 insulin-like growth factor receptor (IGF-1R) are frequently amplified in GBM and the downstream PI3K/Akt pathway is altered in 86–89.6% of GBMs, identifying the latter as a potential therapeutic target.4 Overexpression of IGF-1R has been linked to poorer survival in GBM patients.5 Moreover, IGF-signaling was implicated in resistance of GBM cells to EGFR6 and PDGFR inhibitors7 (reviewed in8).

The ligands, insulin-like growth factors (IGF-1 and IGF-2) are involved in cell growth and differentiation. Ligand binding triggers IGF-1R signaling via the PI3K/Akt and MEK/ERK pathways and nuclear IGF-1R transport to activate gene transcription, thereby regulating resistance to apoptosis, cell proliferation, and cell cycle progression and promoting tumor growth.9,10 We and others have shown that IGF-1R targeting inhibits the growth of GBM cells in vitro and in vivo.9 Recently, we reported that glioma cells with genetically engineered downregulation of IGF-1R implanted orthotopically in the brain had a significantly increased apoptotic rate and their intracerebral growth was inhibited.11 However, to date, IGF-1R targeting in GBM has not advanced to clinical practice.

We previously reported on the bioengineering of a potent IGF-1R signaling inhibitor, the IGF-Trap—a fusion protein consisting of the entire extracellular domain of the human IGF-1R fused to the Fc domain of human IgG1. The IGF-Trap binds to IGF-1 and IGF-2 (but not insulin) with high affinity, thereby reducing ligand bioavailability to the cognate receptor and impeding receptor activation. We have shown that the IGF-Trap blocked IGF-1R phosphorylation and signaling in tumor cells in vitro and in vivo and inhibited the growth of several very aggressive carcinomas in vivo including colon, lung, and pancreatic carcinoma cells.12 A highly effective variant of the IGF-Trap with increased stability and efficacy was recently engineered13 (reviewed in14). The effect of this inhibitor on GBM growth remained to be assessed.

One major challenge to successful treatment of GBM and other brain malignancies is effective drug delivery to the brain, as drug exclusion by the blood–brain barrier (BBB) limits drug access to the tumor. The BBB is a semi-permeable layer of specialized endothelial cells as well as astrocytic end-feet processes and basement membrane that protect the brain from foreign and potentially harmful substances.15 Strategies for increasing drug diffusion through the BBB for effective delivery of large molecules such as biologics are therefore actively being sought. Trimethyl chitosan nanoparticles (NP) termed TRIOZAN™ have enhanced transcytosis, due to their positively charged moiety and were shown to improve uptake of their cargo in the brain.16 In this study, we used human and murine pre-clinical GBM models to assess the efficacy of direct intracerebral injection of the IGF-Trap on glioma growth in vivo and evaluated the benefit of IGF-Trap encapsulation in TRIOZAN™ nanoparticles (NPs) for delivering therapeutically effective doses of the IGF-Trap to the brain to treat intra-cerebrally implanted GBM tumors.

sec.title: Cells
sec.p: Human U87MG and mouse GL261 glioma cells were obtained from the ATCC and the DTP/DCTD/NCI Tumor Repository, respectively. The use of these cells as GBM models has been extensively reviewed elsewhere.17 The cells were cultured at 37 °C in DMEM medium (Wisent) supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum FBS (Wisent) and antibiotics. As per the McGill University Animal Care Committee and the McGill University Biohazard committee guidelines, they were periodically tested for mouse and human pathogens and mycoplasma infection, and were last retested in 2021 during the course of these studies. To avoid cross-contamination and phenotype changes, these cell lines were not propagated in long-term cultures. Following acquisition from the tumor repositories, they were expanded, maintained as frozen stocks, and cultured for 2–4 weeks only before they were injected, to preserve the tumorigenic phenotype. The origin and phenotype of human glioma stem cell line MES-GSC1123 (MES-1123) were described in detail elsewhere. The line was established by the coauthor (I.N.) within 5 years of its initial publication in 201318 and was received as a kind gift and maintained in the Rak laboratory.19 These cells represent the mesenchymal GSC subtype. They are highly aggressive upon intracerebral implantation, highly resistant to radiation, and acquire Tomozolomide-resistance upon treatment in vivo, mimicking the clinical manifestations of aggressive GBM. Transcriptomic data on these cells can be found in.19,20 They were cultured (as neurospheres) in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium/F12 supplemented with B27 (2%), Glutamax, epidermal growth factor (20 ng/ml), basic fibroblast growth factor (20 ng/ml), penicillin/streptomycin (Life Technologies), and heparin 5 μg/ml (Stem Cell Technologies) for 7–14 days only prior to injection intra-cerebrally, as indicated. All cells were cultured overnight in full media and then washed twice in serum-free media before their injection. The immortalized normal human astrocyte line NHA was originally obtained from the late Dr. Guha (University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario)21 and validated in the Rak laboratory.22,23 These cells were cultured in DMEM medium with 10% FBS and 1% Penicillin-streptomycin.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: All mouse experiments were carried out in strict accordance with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care (CCAC) “Guide to the Care and Use of Experimental Animals” and under the conditions and procedures approved by the Animal Care Committee of McGill University (AUP number: 5733). All mice were bred in the animal facility of the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Center and used for the experiments at the ages of 7–12 weeks old. The experiments were performed in male (or as indicated) NSG mice (for U87 MG, MES-1123, and orthotopic GL261 injections) or in syngeneic C57Bl/6 mice (for subcutaneous GL261 injections).

sec.title: The IGF-Trap
sec.p: The IGF-Trap is a fusion protein consisting of the entire extracellular domain of the human IGF-1R fused to the Fc portion of human IgG1. Similarly to the cognate receptor, the IGF-Trap binds the ligands IGF-1 and IGF-2 (but not insulin) with high affinity, reducing ligand bioavailability in the circulation. The bioengineering and properties of the IGF-Trap were described in detail previously,24 and also reviewed extensively in.14 The bioengineering of a 3rd generation IGF-Trap with improved physicochemical and pharmacodynamic properties was described recently.13 This Trap (IGF-Trap 3.3) was used in all the experiments.

sec.title: MTT Assay
sec.p: Glioma cells were seeded in 96-well plates and incubated for 24 h at 37 °C in full medium. The medium was then replaced with FBS-free medium containing, or not, 10 ng/ml of IGF-1 and in the presence or absence of IGF-Trap, at the indicated molar ratios to IGF-1. The cells were incubated for up to 96 hours and the increase in cell numbers was analyzed every 24 h by quantifying formazan crystals reduced by the NAD(P)H-dependent oxidoreductase enzyme—an indicator of metabolic activity. Absorbance at 570nm was measured using the Infinite 200 PRO microplate reader (TECAN Switzerland, Morrisville, NC, USA).

sec.title: Cell Cycle Analysis
sec.p: Cell cycle progression was analyzed by flow cytometry. Cells in 6-well plates (5 × 104 cells/well) were serum starved (in DMEM) overnight for 18 h before treatment for 24 h with 50 ng/ml IGF-1 and with and without IGF-Trap used at a 3:1 molar ratio to IGF-1. Cells were collected, centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 min, washed twice with PBS, and fixed overnight in chilled 70% ethanol. Cells were stained with 50 μg/ml propidium iodide, and treated with 100 μg/ml RNase A for 2 h at 4 °C in the dark, and debris removed using a cell strainer (pore size 100 μm) before the analysis. Cell cycle phases were determined by acquiring at least 104 events using the FACSCanto (BD Biosciences, San Jose, CA, USA), and the data were analyzed using the FlowJo software.

sec.title: Subcutaneous Tumor Cell Injection
sec.p: U87MG or GL261 cells (1 × 106 cells/mouse) were injected subcutaneously into the right flank of NSG and C5Bl/6 male mice, respectively. Mice were randomized for treatment when the tumors were palpable and received bi-weekly i.v. injection of 5 (GL261) or 7.5 (U87MG) mg/kg IGF-Trap or vehicle as control. The tumors were measured twice weekly using a caliper and the volume was calculated using the formula Volume = length2 × width/2. Treatments ceased when the mean tumor diameter reached 1.5 cm and the mice were sacrificed at end point, as per the McGill Animal Care Committee guidelines.

sec.title: Intracranial Tumor Implantation and Cannulation
sec.p: U87MG (2 × 105 cells/mouse), GL261 (1 × 105) or MES-1123 (2.5 × 104) cells expressing the Luciferase gene were used for intracerebral tumor injection. The cells were injected orthotopically into the cerebral cortex using a Stoelting stereotactic apparatus at coordinates (−2, −1, −3.5) of Bregma. A cannula (328OPM/Spc, P1 technologies, Roanoke, VA USA) was implanted above the tumor injection site for repeated, direct injection of 5 μg IGF-Trap (or vehicle) into the brains in proximity to the tumor site. Longitudinal bioluminescence imaging was performed with the IVIS Spectrum/200 (PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA, USA), following intraperitoneal injection of the mice with 150 mg/kg XenoLight RediJect D-Luciferin (Caliper Lifesciences; Caliper/PerkinElmer). Treatment continued until humane end point.

sec.title: Encapsulation of the IGF-Trap in TRIOZAN™ Nanoparticles
sec.p: TRIOZAN™ nanoparticles (commercialized by Ovensa Inc.) were formed as an ionic complex between the polysaccharides trimethylamine chitosan (TRIOZAN™, Mw > 50 kDa, degree of quaternization > 50%) - a cationic biopolymer and sodium dextran sulfate (DS) - an anionic biopolymer, mixed with the ionic gelation agent tripolyphosphate (TPP) at a fixed TRIOZAN:DS:TPP ratio. A microfluidic chip with controlled flow rates (Precision NanoSystems, Vancouver, BC, Canada) was used to improve reproducibility between preparations. In this complex, TRIOZAN™ is added in excess to the negatively charged polymers, to retain a positive overall surface charge. The zeta-potential of the nanoparticles was measured and was equal to +14.4 ±0.7 mV in PBS pH 7.4, consistent with a surface composition of trimethyl chitosan.

Nanoparticle encapsulation of the IGF-Trap was achieved by precipitating the two polyelectrolytes to form complexes (PEC) in the presence of IGF-Trap. Excess, non-encapsulated IGF-Trap was removed by centrifugation (30 min at 42,000g in a refrigerated centrifuge) to separate the nanoparticles from the free polymers and non-encapsulated proteins. The nanoparticles in the pellet were resuspended in PBS. Quantification of the encapsulated IGF-Trap was assessed by SDS-PAGE using non-encapsulated IGF-Trap as a standard and where indicated, the concentration was adjusted to deliver comparable doses of free and encapsulated IGF-Trap. Nanoparticles were stable in vitro for several months when maintained in physiological saline solutions. However, once encapsulation of IGF-Trap was performed, the nanoparticles were used within 2–3 weeks.

To enable detection of the IGF-Trap in vivo, it was conjugated to a near-infrared fluorescent dye (CF680R-succinimide) using an average of 2 dye molecules/IGF-Trap (λex 680 nm/λem 701 nm), as per the manufacturer’s instructions (Biotium, Fremont CA, USA). The CF™680R succinimide ester (NHS-CF™680) was covalently bound to primary amines of IGF-Trap. The mixture of the IGF-Trap with the CF™ dye was agitated for 1h at room temperature, pH 8.0, and the fluorescently labeled IGF-Trap was purified from excess free CF™680R using an Amicon centrifugal filter Eppendorf tube with a 10 kDa molecular weight cutoff, and rinsed 4 times with fresh PBS. The labeled protein was detectable by confocal microscopy performed on frozen sections and by optical imaging in live animals using the IVIS Spectrum/200.

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry
sec.p: NSG mice were injected with IGF-Trap that was pre-labeled with a fluorescent tag (CF680R (λex 680nm/λem 701 nm) and NP-encapsulated, or not (free IGF-Trap). The animals were sacrificed and the brains removed, 1–12 hr post injection and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, followed by a 3 day incubation in a 30% sucrose solution. The brains were then snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen and cryostat sections of 10 μm thickness were prepared. The sections were immunostained with a rat anti-mouse CD31 antibody (BD Biosciences, cat# 550,274) followed by an AF488-conjugated anti-rat IgG secondary antibody (λex 490 nm/λem 525 nm, Invitrogen) to visualize blood vessels, counterstained with DAPI and mounted in the ProLong Gold mounting reagent. Fluorescent images were acquired with a Zeiss LSM780 laser scanning confocal microscope equipped with an AxioCam camera, and analyzed by ImageJ.

sec.title: Treatment of Tumor Bearing Mice With the NP-Encapsulated IGF-Trap
sec.p: Male NSG mice were randomized into 3 treatment groups for injection i.v. with NP-Trap, free IGF-Trap (5 mg/kg), or vehicle (PBS). Treatment began 3 and 1 days prior to intracranial injection of 106 GL261 cells in 3 μl PBS, using the coordinates described above, and continued twice weekly thereafter, from day 3 post tumor injection onward for a total of 10 treatments per mouse. Mice were imaged once weekly using the IVIS Spectrum/200, as described. Following the last IGF-Trap injection, the mice were monitored twice weekly until moribund, at which time they were sacrificed.

sec.title: Western Blotting
sec.p: Cells (as indicated) were lysed using the RIPA buffer (50mM Tris (pH 7.4), 1mM EDTA, 150mM NaCl, 1% (w/v) NP-40, 2mM Na3VO4, 5mM NaF, 0.25% sodium deoxycholate) containing a Protease Inhibitor Cocktail for 30 min at 4 °C. Protein lysates were centrifuged at 13,000g for 20 min and 20 μg proteins/lane were loaded onto 10% polyacrylamide gels, transferred onto Nitrocellulose membranes, and probed first overnight at 4 °C, with an antibody IGF-1R (Abcam, ab182408) diluted 1:1000 in TBST (Tris buffered saline with 0.1% Tween) containing 5% BSA and then for 1h at RT with an HRP-conjugated secondary antibody diluted 1:5000. β-actin detected with a monoclonal anti β-actin antibody (Millipore Sigma cat# A5441) was used as a loading control. Signals were detected using the Thermo Scientific™ SuperSignal™ West Pico PLUS Chemilluminescent Substrate. Signal detection and densitometry were performed using ImageQuant Las4000.

sec.title: Statistical Analyses
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 6. The one-way ANOVA (post-hoc test) was used to analyze results of in vitro MTT assays, the student’s t test to analyze tumor measurements and the Gehan-Brewslow-Wilcoxon test to analyze Kaplan Meier survival curves.

sec.title: The IGF-Trap Inhibits IGF-1 Induced Glioma Cell Proliferation In Vitro
sec.p: We began by evaluating the effect of the IGF-Trap on glioma growth in vitro. GL261 and U87 MG cells were selected for this study because they are highly aggressive in vivo and recapitulate GBM phenotypes and drug responses.17 Moreover, in our previous studies we have already shown that intracerebral growth of U87MG cells was IGF-1R expression dependent,9 and IGF-1R overexpression as compared to normal human astrocytes was confirmed in both U87MG and GL261 with levels particularly high in the latter. (Supplementary Figure 1). To confirm the IGF-Trap sensitivity of these cells, we first tested its effect in vitro using an MTT assay. Cells were cultured in minimal (1%) FBS medium containing, or not, 10 ng/ml IGF-1 and with or without IGF-Trap that was used at a molar ratio of 1:1 and 1:2 (IGF-1: IGF-Trap). We found that cell density significantly increased in medium containing a minimal serum concentration supplemented with IGF-1 only. Similarly to our previously published results with pediatric high-grade glioma cells,25 this increased proliferation was blocked by the addition of the IGF-Trap (Figure 1), confirming IGF-1 responsiveness of these cells and the inhibitory effect of the IGF-Trap. We also noted that cell growth resumed when treatment with IGF-Trap ended, suggesting that resistant subpopulation may have emerged following treatment cessation. Moreover, similarly to our findings with the human pediatric glioblastoma DIPG13 cells,25 we found that IGF-1 enhanced cell cycle progression of GL261 cells relative to controls and that IGF-Trap blocked G1-S transition of these cells (Supplementary Figure 2), raising the possibility that treatment cessation, enabled return to cell cycling for these cells.

sec.title: The IGF-Trap Inhibits Subcutaneous Growth of Glioma Cells
sec.p: To evaluate the therapeutic effect of IGF-Trap in vivo, we began with a subcutaneous (s.c.) tumor model where tumor growth can be more directly measured. Syngeneic C57Bl/6 and NSG male mice were inoculated s.c. with 106 GL261 and U87MG cells, respectively. When tumors were palpable, mice were randomized into control and IGF-Trap treatment groups and received two weekly i.v. injections of vehicle (PBS), 5 mg/kg (GL261), or 7.5 mg/kg (U87MG) IGF-Trap. Tumors were measured using a caliper and tumor volumes were calculated (Figure 2A). The treatment continued until mice in the control group reached end point (one of tumor diameters exceeded 1.5 cm or mice were moribund). In all mice injected with GL261 cells and treated with the IGF-Trap, we observed a significant decrease in the tumor growth rate, as compared to controls, and this continued until the experiment was terminated. By day 60 post tumor cell injection, all vehicle-treated GL261-injected mice were moribund, whereas 60% of mice treated with IGF-Trap were still alive (Figure 2B and C). Similar results were obtained in NSG mice injected subcutaneously with U87MG cells. In this group, we observed a significant inhibition of tumor growth in IGF-Trap-treated mice throughout the treatment period and this resulted in increased survival (Figure 2D and E).

sec.title: Direct Intracerebral Administration of IGF-Trap Inhibits Glioma Growth in the Brain And Extends Survival
sec.p: Having established the sensitivity of the tumor cells to IGF-Trap treatment in vitro and in vivo, we next sought to determine whether their growth in the brain could also be blocked by the IGF-Trap. To overcome the likely exclusion of circulating IGF-Trap from the brain by the BBB, we administered the IGF-Trap directly into the brain via a cannula implanted intracerebrally. GL261 cells expressing the luciferase gene were injected orthotopically into the brain (105 cells/mouse), using a stereotactic instrument and the mice were randomized 3 days later, based on the bioluminescent signal detected by optical imaging. Guided by tumor implantation coordinates, a cannula was then implanted into the brain and used to deliver 5 μg IGF-Trap (or vehicle), twice weekly, from day 3 onward. Tumor growth was monitored twice weekly using optical imaging (Figure 3A). We found that while all mice in the control group (4/4) developed detectable tumors by day 17 that progressed rapidly thereafter, tumors in the IGF-Trap-treated group were only detectable in 1/5 mice at that time, and the growth rate in the majority of treated mice was lower than in the control group, although the difference under these experimental conditions did not reach statistical significance (defined as P ≤ 0.05) (Figure 3B). This resulted in median survival of 54 and 63 days in the control and IGF-treated groups, respectively (Figure 3C), but overall survival, as assessed by the Gehan-Brewslow-Wilcoxon test was not significantly improved. A more uniform response was seen in mice injected with U87MG cells. Male NSG mice were implanted intracerebrally with 2 × 105 cells and randomized on day 3. IGF-Trap (5 µg/treatment) was administered via a cannula twice weekly from day 3 onward for 5 weeks. IGF-Trap treatment significantly reduced intracerebral growth of the U87MG tumors (Figure 3D) and this resulted in a significantly increased survival for the treated (median survival time 97 days), as compared to control (median survival time 49 days) mice, as shown in the Kaplan Meier survival curves (Figure 3E).

sec.title: The IGF-Trap Also Inhibits the Growth of Human Glioma Stem Cells
sec.p: We confirmed the inhibitory effect of IGF-Trap using GBM stem cell (GSC) xenografts growing in NSG mice. Mice were injected orthotopically with the very aggressive human glioma stem cells (GSC) MES-1123 and treated as described above. Untreated mice implanted intra-cranially with 2.5 × 104 MES-1123 cells developed intracerebral tumors rapidly and all reached the clinical end point by 12 days post injection. sec.title: Nanoparticle Encapsulation Improves Systemic Delivery of the IGF-Trap to the Brain
sec.p: Continuous drug administration via a cerebrally implanted cannula, while it may be effective in delivering the drug to the tumor site, is challenging in the clinical setting. Optimally, drugs should access the brain from the circulation in high enough concentrations to affect local tumor growth. However, access to large biologics such as antibodies and the IGF-Trap is hindered by the BBB. Strategies to increase penetrability of biologics into the brain for the treatment of malignant disease are therefore actively being sought. We selected to use a nanoparticle (NP)-based delivery approach for increased IGF-Trap delivery and retention in the brain. Nanocarriers have the added advantage of decreasing drug uptake and opsonization by the mononuclear phagocytic system (MPS).26,27

TRIOZAN™, is a polymeric nanocarrier that enables the encapsulation and protection of targeted drugs (small molecules and biologics) and was shown to improve drug delivery across the BBB.28 We therefore encapsulated the IGF-Trap in TRIOZAN™ nanoparticles and confirmed the integrity of the protein within this nanocarrier, using gel electrophoresis (Supplementary Figure 3). To enable detection of the IGF-Trap in the brain, we pre-labeled the IGF-Trap with a CF680 fluorescent dye. Mice were injected intravenously with 100 μg of the fluorescently tagged IGF-Trap that was either free or NP-encapsulated (NP-Trap, adjusted to contain 100 μg IGF-Trap protein), and optical imaging was used to monitor the fluorescent signal over a period of 24 hr. As expected, we observed a high concentration of the labeled IGF-Trap in the livers of all mice at 5 minutes postinjection, and a detectable signal was also observed in the brain. However, while in mice injected with free IGF-Trap, the signal was weak or no longer detectable by 4 hr, it was still detectable in the brains of NP-Trap injected mice at 24 hr post injection (Figure 5A), suggesting that TRIOZAN™ encapsulation improved brain retention of the IGF-Trap. This was also evident when the fluorescent signal intensity was measured and normalized to signal intensity at 5 min (0.083 hr, as shown in Figure 5A-extreme left panel). While 90% of the signal detectable at 5 min was still observed 24 hr post NP-Trap injection, only ≤ 50% of the free IGF-Trap was still detectable at that time (Figure 5B). Ex vivo imaging of brains resected 1 hr post injection also revealed a stronger (although not statistically significant) fluorescent signal in mice injected with NP-Trap, as compared to non-encapsulated IGF-Trap (Supplementary Figure 4). Together, the data indicated that TRIOZAN™ encapsulation improved IGF-Trap retention and thereby, its bioavailability in the brain.

Within 1 hr of the injection, fluorescently labeled IGF-Trap could be observed within, or in proximity to brain blood vessels, in both treatment groups (Figure 5C-left-white arrows). However, while the fluorescent signal declined rapidly and was undetectable in the brains of IGF-Trap-injected mice by 4 hr, it was observed within, and adjacent to blood vessels of NP-IGF-Trap treated mice at 4 hr (Figure 5C) and a weak signal was still detectable 12 hr postinjection in these mice (Supplementary Figure 5).

sec.title: Systemic Administration of Nanoparticle-Encapsulated IGF-Trap Inhibits Intracerebral Glioma Growth
sec.p: Finally, having documented a more prolonged retention of NP-encapsulated IGF-Trap in the brain and localization within, and adjacent to vascular structures, we assessed the effect of the encapsulated IGF-Trap on intracerebral tumor growth. Mice were injected intracerebrally with GL261 cells and treated with encapsulated or free IGF-Trap, using the regimen outlined in Figure 6A. Initial attempts to treat the mice post intra-cerebral implantation of the tumor cells did not result in a significant decrease in the rate of tumor growth. We rationed that this may be due to a combination of factors namely, the aggressive nature and rapid growth of these cells in the brain, the paracrine stimulation of tumor cell growth by locally produced IGF-1 and IGF-229,30 and the added challenge of calibrating the precise levels of IGF-Trap released from the nanoparticles in the brain. We, therefore, pretreated the mice with IGF-Trap or NP-Trap in order to reduce the bioavailability of local IGF prior to tumor injection (Figure 6A), while also ascertaining the efficacy of this approach for delivery of the drug to the brain following systemic inoculation. Mice were imaged twice weekly to monitor tumor growth. We observed no treatment-related toxicity in mice injected systemically with either free or NP-encapsulated IGF-Trap. We found that NP-Trap (but not free IGF-Trap) significantly reduced intracerebral tumor growth, as compared to vehicle-treated control mice (Figure 6B and C). This effect was evident while the IGF-Trap was administered and was reflected in a significant extension to animal survival, as compared to mice treated with either the vehicle or free IGF-Trap (Figure 6D). Cessation of treatment (Day 27) accelerated tumor growth in all treated mice, suggesting that when administered as monotherapy, maintenance of high IGF-Trap levels in the brain and circulation is essential for long-term blockade of tumor growth.

sec.title: iscussion
sec.p: Drug delivery to the brain remains a major challenge due to the limited diffusion through the BBB and strategies are therefore being sought for transiently breaching the BBB to increase drug access to the brain for the treatment of primary and metastatic tumors.31–33 We have documented increased brain penetration of the IGF-Trap using high-amplitude repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS)34 and have recently reported on the increased therapeutic potency of the IGF-Trap when combined with rTMS for the treatment of intra-cerebrally implanted glioma cells.35

Here we show that the intracerebral growth of aggressive human gliomas and patient-derived glioma stem cells could be inhibited by the direct intracranial administration of the IGF-Trap, consistent with the documented role of the IGF- axis in glioma progression. Of note are our results with MES-1123—the highly aggressive patient-derived glioma stem cells. We found a modest (but significant) increase in the survival of mice injected orthotopically with these cells, when treated with the IGF-Trap. In view of their rapid growth, whereby all control mice were at humane end point by 12 days post injection, our results suggest that targeting the IGF-axis may be clinically beneficial, particularly if enough of the drug can reach the tumor site. Similar results were reported by Zamykal et al, using mice that were orthotopically implanted with U87 cells and treated with the IGF-1R targeting antibody IMC-A12 delivered to the tumor site via an intra-cerebrally implanted catheter.36 Of note, IGF-Trap administered directly into the brain had a variable effect on intra-cerebral growth of murine GL261 cells and did not significantly improve overall survival, although we did observe a significant effect on GL261 tumors growing subcutaneously and in mice pretreated systemically with NP-Trap, prior to intra-cerebral tumor injection. This may be due to the relatively high IGF-1R expression on these cells and the paracrine growth-stimulating effect of high local IGF levels in the brain.29,30 Further optimization of the treatment protocol including combination of the treatment with other modalities such as radiation and chemotherapy may be required to improve the outcome in this model.
Continuous direct intracranial drug delivery is clinically challenging. We therefore sought to use a non-invasive method to optimize the potential clinical utility of the IGF-Trap for GBM treatment.

Nanomedicine has emerged as an important platform for increasing drug delivery and efficacy for cancer treatment.37 TRIOZANTM is a nanoparticle delivery vehicle based on a chitosan derivative, N-trimethyl chitosan. It encapsulates and associates with target molecules to increase their diffusion into a tumor site and can protect them from degradation, thereby increasing their stability in vivo. TRIOZANTM nanoparticles have mucoadhesive properties and a surface charge similar to the chitosan nanoparticles but are soluble at a wider pH range because chemical modification of some of the amines results in a permanent positive charge that confers stability even in very basic pH, due to inter-chain repulsion. Ionic interactions between these cationic nanocarriers and the endothelial cells and their sub-micron size facilitate crossing of the BBB by the NP carrier and its cargo via absorptive-mediated transcytosis.16,38 Because the IGF-Trap is associated with the polysaccharide carrier but not covalently attached, it can be released intact from the NP through diffusion or as the carrier is degraded. Hence, TRIOZANTM was shown to increase the accumulation of therapeutics in targeted tissues including the brain, where it increased drug penetration of the BBB.28,39 Indeed, we found that TRIOZAN™- encapsulation increased IGF-Trap retention in the brain in comparison to the free molecule. Moreover, using immunohistochemistry, we localized the IGF-Trap within, and adjacent to vascular structures in the brain, suggesting that encapsulation enabled diffusion of this inhibitor through the BBB.

In contrast to other studies where the levels of N-trimethyl chitosan-encapsulated agents in the brain were evaluated postmortem,40 we were able to visualize IGF-Trap distribution longitudinally in live animals using optical imaging, allowing us to identify a clear difference between the biodistribution of the encapsulated and free drug. This method can therefore be used in the future to further optimize the ratio of the drug to N-trimethyl chitosan in order to increase even further the therapeutic potency of NP-encapsulated IGF-Trap. Of note, this method of detection cannot adjust for potential fluorescent signal quenching by N-trimethyl chitosan nanoparticles. Our ex–vivo measurement based on the linear range of the standard curve (Supplementary Figure 6) suggests, however, that the detection efficiency of the fluorescent signal was 2-fold higher for free than for encapsulated IGF-Trap. This implies that the difference in the bioavailability of the two IGF-Trap formulations was even greater than detectable by optical imaging of live animals.

We observed that the injection of free IGF-Trap intravenously also reduced the intracerebral growth of the GL261 tumors, although the effect did not reach statistical significance when compared to vehicle-treated mice. This, more modest, effect may be due to the reduction in the bioavailability of circulating IGF-1 and IGF-2 that can cross the BBB due to their small size (7–7.5 kD)41 and may contribute to tumor growth in the brain. The relative contributions of local and systemic IGF ligands to intracerebral tumor growth are unknown, but the increased therapeutic effect of NP-Trap suggests that the local ligands play a major role.

In this study, when administering IGF-Trap systemically (as free IGF-Trap or NP-encapsulated), we pretreated the mice prior to intracerebral tumor cell injection in order to reduce the bioavailability of locally produced ligands in the brain. We therefore cannot rule out the possibility that IGF-Trap in this setting, also affected initial tumor cell engraftment in the brain. Although this treatment regimen is obviously impracticable in the clinical setting for the management of primary GBM, it may have utility in prevention of tumor recurrence. Furthermore, in this study, we used IGF-Trap as a monotherapy. In the clinical setting, given the aggressive nature of this disease, IGF-Trap is likely to be most effective when combined with other modalities such as surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation. In those settings, when tumor volume is reduced and its outgrowth is inhibited by additional treatment regimens, pretreatment with IGF-Trap or long-term sustained treatment may not be required to achieve optimal disease management.

Other studies have also documented increased drug delivery and potency when the target agents were encapsulated in trimethyl chitosan-based formulations. For example, trimethyl chitosan-encapsulated retinoic acid was used to treat glioblastoma cells in vitro and this resulted in increased cytotoxicity, apoptosis, and necrosis.42 Chitosan-based nanoparticles were also used to enhance the bioavailability of anti-cancer drugs such as 5-fluorouracil,43 paclitaxel,44 and cytarabine45 with demonstrated increased bioavailability. In rats injected subcutaneously with cytarabine encapsulated in chitosan microspheres, cytarabine could be detected in the plasma for 13 days,45 and in diabetic rats injected with chitosan nanoparticles-encapsulated insulin, an enhanced intestinal absorption of insulin and a prolonged hypoglycemic effect were observed.46 However, to our knowledge, ours is the first demonstration of improved delivery and increased bioavailability of a large biological drug such as the IGF-Trap (approximately 390 kDa) to the brain by trimethyl chitosan encapsulation, for the treatment of a brain malignancy.

Finally, our findings may have clinical implications beyond the treatment of GBM, as nanomedicine may enable delivery of targeted drugs to the brain for the treatment of metastases from other malignancies such as breast carcinoma and melanoma, where antibodies and other drugs with known therapeutic efficacy against the primary tumor and non-cerebral metastases are already in routine use in the clinic.
